q: Ana has two orders, Ben has one, and Cy and Dee have none. How many rows does this inner join return?
code:
-- customers(id, name): (1,'Ana'), (2,'Ben'), (3,'Cy'), (4,'Dee')
-- orders(id, customer_id): (10,1), (11,1), (12,2)
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
why: An inner join returns one row for every pair of rows that satisfies ON. Ana matches two orders, Ben matches one, and Cy and Dee match nothing, so they are left out: 2 + 1 = 3 rows.
wrong: An inner join does not return one row per customer. Customers with no match are dropped, and Ana appears twice.
Rows are not merged per customer. Each matching pair is its own row, so Ana's two orders give two rows.
That is 4 customers times 3 orders, the CROSS JOIN count. The ON condition keeps only the matching pairs.

q: Ana has two orders, Ben has one, and Cy and Dee have none. This query uses a LEFT JOIN. What does the result contain?
code:
-- customers(id, name): (1,'Ana'), (2,'Ben'), (3,'Cy'), (4,'Dee')
-- orders(id, customer_id): (10,1), (11,1), (12,2)
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
options: 5 rows; Cy and Dee appear once each, with NULL in o.id
4 rows; a LEFT JOIN returns exactly one row per customer
3 rows; customers without orders are still left out
5 rows; Cy and Dee appear once each, with 0 in o.id
why: A LEFT JOIN returns every match an inner join would, plus each left row that matched nothing, padded with NULL on the right. That is Ana twice, Ben once, then Cy and Dee once each: 5 rows.
wrong: LEFT JOIN guarantees at least one row per customer, not exactly one. Ana matches two orders, so she appears twice.
That is the inner join result. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills the right side with NULL.
Missing values are filled with NULL, not 0. NULL here means there is no matching row at all.

q: A report must list every customer with their orders, and customers who never ordered must still appear. Which FROM clause fits?
options: customers JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
customers LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
customers RIGHT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
customers CROSS JOIN orders
why: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the table on its left. A customer with orders gets one row per order; a customer with none gets one row with NULL in the order columns.
wrong: A plain (inner) join keeps only customers with at least one order, so the ones who never ordered vanish.
RIGHT JOIN keeps every order, not every customer. Customers with no orders are still missing.
CROSS JOIN pairs every customer with every order, including orders that belong to someone else.

q: Ana has an order of 100, Ben an order of 20, and Cy no orders. The query uses a LEFT JOIN but filters o.amount in WHERE. Which names come back?
code:
-- customers(id, name): (1,'Ana'), (2,'Ben'), (3,'Cy')
-- orders(customer_id, amount): (1,100), (2,20)
SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.amount > 50;
options: Ana, Ben and Cy
Ana and Cy
An error: WHERE cannot use a column from the right side of a LEFT JOIN
Ana only
why: WHERE runs after the join. Ben's row fails 20 > 50, and Cy's row has o.amount NULL, so NULL > 50 is unknown and the row is dropped. The LEFT JOIN ends up acting like an inner join. To keep every customer, put the condition in ON.
wrong: That is the result with AND o.amount > 50 inside ON. In WHERE, the filter runs after the join and removes rows.
Cy's row has o.amount NULL, and NULL > 50 is not true, so WHERE removes Cy as well.
WHERE may use any joined column. The query is legal; it just means something else than intended.

q: Starting from customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id, which WHERE clause returns only the customers who have never ordered?
options: WHERE o.id IS NULL
WHERE o.id = NULL
WHERE c.id IS NULL
WHERE o.customer_id <> c.id
why: For a customer with no orders, the LEFT JOIN produces one row whose order columns are all NULL. Keeping only rows where o.id IS NULL leaves exactly those customers. This is called an anti-join; NOT EXISTS is another way to write it.
wrong: A comparison with NULL is never true, so = NULL matches no rows. Testing for a missing value needs IS NULL.
c.id comes from customers and is filled in for every customer. Only the right side gets NULL padding.
Matched rows are equal by the ON clause, and for unmatched rows NULL <> c.id is unknown, not true. Nothing comes back.

q: A product has 2 tags and 3 reviews. The query joins the product to both child tables at once. How many rows come back?
code:
-- products(id, name): (1,'Lamp')
-- tags(product_id, tag): (1,'home'), (1,'light')
-- reviews(product_id, stars): (1,4), (1,5), (1,3)
SELECT p.name, t.tag, r.stars
FROM products p
JOIN tags t ON t.product_id = p.id
JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id;
why: Both child tables match on the product, not on each other, so every tag pairs with every review: 2 x 3 = 6 rows. This fan-out is why a SUM or COUNT over such a join comes out too large.
wrong: Joins do not add up the rows of each table. Each tag is paired with each review.
The tags do not just ride along on the review rows; every review row is repeated once per tag.
Joining never collapses a product into one row. That takes GROUP BY.

q: Ada is the CEO, so her manager_id is NULL. Bo and Cy report to Ada. What does this self join return?
code:
-- employees(id, name, manager_id):
--   (1,'Ada',NULL), (2,'Bo',1), (3,'Cy',1)
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
options: Three rows, with Ada's manager shown as NULL
Two rows: Bo with Ada, and Cy with Ada
One row: Ada, the only manager in the table
An error, because a table cannot be joined to itself
why: The aliases e and m let the query treat employees as two tables. Bo and Cy each find Ada as their manager. Ada's manager_id is NULL, which equals nothing, so the inner join leaves her out.
wrong: That needs a LEFT JOIN. An inner join drops Ada, because her NULL manager_id matches no id.
Each employee row is matched on its own. The query lists employees with their managers, not distinct managers.
A table can be joined to itself by giving it two aliases, here e and m.

q: You want only the departments whose average salary is above 5000. Where does the condition AVG(salary) > 5000 belong?
options: In WHERE, before GROUP BY
In ORDER BY, after the groups are built
In GROUP BY, as GROUP BY AVG(salary) > 5000
In HAVING, after the groups are formed
why: The database filters rows (WHERE), then forms groups (GROUP BY), then filters groups (HAVING). An average only exists once its group exists, so a condition on AVG has to go in HAVING.
wrong: WHERE filters single rows before any groups exist, so it cannot use AVG. The database rejects it.
ORDER BY only sorts the result. It never removes rows.
GROUP BY decides how rows are grouped. It does not filter, and it cannot contain an aggregate.

q: One of four users has no email (NULL). What does this query return?
code:
-- users(id, email):
--   (1,'a@x.io'), (2,NULL),
--   (3,'c@x.io'), (4,'d@x.io')
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(email)
FROM users;
options: 4 and 3
4 and 4
3 and 3
3 and 4
why: COUNT(*) counts rows, whatever they contain. COUNT(email) counts only the rows where email is not NULL. Four rows, three emails: 4 and 3.
wrong: COUNT(email) skips rows where email is NULL. Only COUNT(*) counts every row.
COUNT(*) counts rows, not values, so the row with a NULL email still counts.
COUNT(*) never looks at column values, so a NULL cannot lower it. COUNT(email) is the one that skips the NULL.

q: This query has both WHERE and HAVING. Which customers does it return?
code:
-- orders(customer, amount):
--   ('Ana',5), ('Ana',20), ('Ana',30),
--   ('Ben',15), ('Ben',8), ('Cy',50)
SELECT customer, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE amount > 10
GROUP BY customer
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
options: Ana with n = 3, and Ben with n = 2
Ana, Ben and Cy
Ana, with n = 2
No rows, because a query cannot use both WHERE and HAVING
why: WHERE runs first and drops Ana's 5 and Ben's 8. Then groups form: Ana has 2 rows, Ben 1, Cy 1. HAVING keeps groups with at least 2 rows, so only Ana remains, with n = 2.
wrong: HAVING does not count the rows from before WHERE. WHERE has already removed Ana's 5 and Ben's 8.
HAVING removes the groups that fail COUNT(*) >= 2. Ben and Cy have one row each after WHERE.
They are often combined: WHERE filters rows, then HAVING filters the groups built from them.

q: The orders table has 10 rows from 3 different customers. How many rows does SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id return?
options: It depends on how the 10 orders are spread over the customers
why: GROUP BY puts all rows with the same customer_id into one group, and the query returns one row per group. Three customers means three rows, each with that customer's order count.
wrong: GROUP BY folds each group into one row. It does not keep every row with a count next to it.
Without GROUP BY, COUNT(*) gives one total row. With GROUP BY you get one row per group.
The spread only changes the counts. The number of rows is the number of groups.

q: Two queries group employees by dept. One filters with WHERE dept = 'Sales', the other with HAVING dept = 'Sales'. What is true?
options: Same rows, but WHERE is the better place: it filters before grouping
Only HAVING works, because dept is the column being grouped on
Only WHERE works, because HAVING may contain aggregates and nothing else
Different results, because WHERE sees whole groups and HAVING sees single rows
why: A condition on the grouping column gives the same answer in either place. In WHERE, the other departments' rows are dropped before grouping. In HAVING, every group is built first and then most are thrown away.
wrong: WHERE can filter on any column of the row, grouping column or not.
HAVING may also use grouping columns. It is just the later, more wasteful place for this filter.
It is the other way round: WHERE sees rows, HAVING sees groups.

q: Ana has two orders and Ben has none. The query counts orders per customer with COUNT(*) over a LEFT JOIN. What does it return?
code:
-- customers(id, name): (1,'Ana'), (2,'Ben')
-- orders(id, customer_id): (10,1), (11,1)
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
options: Ana 2, Ben 0
Ana 2, and no row for Ben
Ana 2, Ben NULL
Ana 2, Ben 1
why: The LEFT JOIN gives Ben one row whose order columns are NULL. COUNT(*) counts rows, so Ben gets 1. COUNT(o.id) skips NULLs and would give the intended 0.
wrong: That needs COUNT(o.id). Ben still has one joined row, filled with NULL, and COUNT(*) counts it.
The LEFT JOIN keeps Ben's row, so GROUP BY makes a group for him too.
COUNT always returns a number, never NULL.

q: Two of three users have no phone number (NULL). What does this query return?
code:
-- users(id, phone):
--   (1,'555-0101'), (2,NULL), (3,NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM users
WHERE phone = NULL;
options: An error, because NULL cannot follow =
why: NULL means unknown, so phone = NULL is unknown for every row, even rows where phone is NULL. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so nothing is counted. IS NULL is the test for a missing value.
wrong: = NULL never matches, not even a NULL. Use phone IS NULL to find missing values.
A comparison with NULL is not skipped or treated as true. It is unknown, and WHERE drops unknown rows.
It is valid SQL. It just never matches anything.

q: Cy's status is NULL. Which names does this query return?
code:
-- users(name, status):
--   ('Ana','active'), ('Ben','banned'), ('Cy',NULL)
SELECT name
FROM users
WHERE status <> 'banned';
options: Ana and Cy
Ana, Ben and Cy
Ana
No rows, because one NULL in the column makes every comparison unknown
why: For Cy, NULL <> 'banned' is unknown: the database cannot say whether an unknown value differs. WHERE keeps only true rows, so only Ana passes. Rows with NULL quietly drop out of = and <> filters alike.
wrong: NULL <> 'banned' is unknown, not true, so Cy is dropped. Add OR status IS NULL to keep him.
Ben's status is 'banned', so his row fails the condition.
Only the row holding the NULL is affected. Other rows compare their own values as usual.

q: One order has a NULL customer_id. The query is meant to list customers who never ordered. What does it return?
code:
-- customers(id, name): (1,'Ana'), (2,'Ben'), (3,'Cy')
-- orders(customer_id): (1), (NULL)
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
options: No rows
Ben and Cy
Ana, Ben and Cy, as if the filter were ignored
An error, because the subquery returns a NULL
why: id NOT IN (1, NULL) means id <> 1 AND id <> NULL. The second part is unknown for every id, so the whole condition is never true and no row passes. Use NOT EXISTS, or exclude NULLs in the subquery.
wrong: That is what NOT EXISTS returns. With NOT IN, the NULL in the list makes every check unknown.
The NULL does not switch the filter off. It makes the condition unknown, and unknown rows are dropped.
Subqueries may return NULLs. The query runs; the NULL changes the result, not whether it is valid.

q: A rating column holds 10, 20 and NULL in three rows. What does SELECT AVG(rating) return?
options: NULL
An error until the NULL row is removed
why: Aggregate functions other than COUNT(*) skip NULLs. AVG adds 10 and 20 and divides by 2, the number of non-NULL values. If a missing rating should count as 0, write AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)).
wrong: That treats NULL as 0 and divides by 3. AVG skips NULLs instead of counting them as zero.
One NULL does not make the whole aggregate NULL. AVG ignores NULLs and averages the rest.
Aggregates are built to handle NULLs. They simply leave them out.

q: SELECT price + shipping AS total returns NULL for orders where shipping was never set. Which version returns just the price for those orders?
options: The same query with WHERE shipping IS NOT NULL
SELECT price + COALESCE(shipping, 0) AS total
The same query; the NULL is only how the tool displays it
SELECT CAST(price + shipping AS INTEGER) AS total
why: Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: a price plus an unknown amount is still unknown. COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument, so a missing shipping cost counts as 0.
wrong: That hides those orders instead of giving them a total.
The value really is NULL. Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, and code reading the column gets NULL too.
The NULL is not a type problem. Casting NULL still gives NULL.

q: Finding a user by email in a 10 million row table takes seconds. After adding an index on email it takes milliseconds. Why?
options: It loads the whole table into memory, so the scan itself runs faster
It stores each query's result, so repeated lookups are answered from it
It keeps emails sorted with row pointers, so lookups skip the scan
It compresses the table, so a scan has less data to read
why: Without an index the database must check every row. An index (usually a B-tree) keeps the values in sorted order with a pointer to each row, so finding one value takes a few steps, about O(log n) instead of O(n).
wrong: An index is a separate sorted structure. It avoids the scan; it does not speed up reading every row.
That describes a cache. An index speeds up the very first lookup of any email, not only repeats.
An index adds data; it does not shrink the table. The gain comes from skipping rows.

q: A logging table takes thousands of inserts per second and has 8 indexes. Inserts are slow. What is the most likely cause?
options: Each insert must also add an entry to all 8 indexes
Indexes only affect reads, so the cause must be somewhere else
Each insert rebuilds all 8 indexes from scratch
The whole table is re-sorted on disk after every insert
why: An index is an extra sorted copy of some columns. Every insert has to place a new entry in every index, so write cost grows with the number of indexes. Index the columns your queries really search on, not everything.
wrong: Indexes speed up reads but are not free: each one is updated on every insert, update and delete.
An index is updated in place with one new entry. Rebuilding on every insert would be far slower still.
Adding a row does not reorder the existing rows. The extra work is keeping the indexes up to date.

q: A table has one index on (last_name, first_name). Which query gets the least help from it?
options: WHERE last_name = 'Cohen'
WHERE last_name = 'Cohen' AND first_name = 'Dana'
WHERE last_name = 'Cohen' ORDER BY first_name
WHERE first_name = 'Dana'
why: The index is sorted by last_name first, like a phone book. People named Dana are spread across every last name, so the index gives no place to start. A composite index helps when the query fixes a leftmost prefix of its columns.
wrong: last_name is the first column of the index, so the database can jump straight to the Cohens.
Both columns are given, in index order. This is the best case for the index.
Within the Cohens, the index is already sorted by first_name, so it serves both the filter and the sort.

q: email has an index, yet SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'dana@x.io' is slow on a large table. Why?
options: LOWER() runs after the index lookup, so the slowness has another cause
The index is sorted by email, not LOWER(email), so no direct lookup is possible
Indexes are never used in a query that calls any function
The index returns rows in the wrong letter case, so each one must be re-checked by hand
why: The index orders the stored email values. LOWER(email) is a new value computed per row at query time, so the database has to compute it for every row. Store emails in one case, or create an index on LOWER(email).
wrong: The index cannot be searched for a value it does not store, so LOWER has to run on every row first.
A function on the search value is fine, and so is an index built on LOWER(email). The problem is wrapping the indexed column.
An index stores the exact column values. The issue is that it cannot be searched for LOWER(email) at all.

q: name has an index. Can WHERE name LIKE '%son' use it to jump straight to the matching rows?
options: Yes: the database finds 'son' in the index the same way it finds a prefix
No: indexes help with = only, never with any range or partial match
No: the index is ordered by how names start, and '%son' fixes no start
Yes, as long as the % is escaped so the index reads it as text
why: Anderson, Wilson and Olson sit far apart in a list sorted from the first letter, so every entry has to be checked. A pattern with a fixed start, like 'Wil%', covers one contiguous range of the index instead.
wrong: Names ending in 'son' are scattered through a list sorted from the first letter, so there is no range to jump to.
Sorted indexes also serve ranges such as BETWEEN, and a fixed prefix like 'Wil%' can map to a range.
Escaping makes % a literal character, which asks a different question: names that are exactly '%son'.

q: is_active is indexed, and 95% of rows have is_active = 1. The database ignores the index for WHERE is_active = 1. Why is that sensible?
options: Nearly every row matches, so reading the table straight through is cheaper
Indexes cannot be built on a column with only two values
The index is out of date and has to be rebuilt before the database can use it
An index only helps queries that also have ORDER BY
why: An index pays off when it narrows the search to a few rows. When a value matches almost the whole table, one index jump per row costs more than a single pass over the table. The same index would help a lot for is_active = 0, the rare 5%.
wrong: They can be built. They just help little when a value matches most rows.
Indexes are updated on every write. Staleness is not the reason.
An index can serve a filter alone. This filter is just not selective.

q: Nobody created an index on orders, yet SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 42 is fast on 10 million rows. id is the primary key. Why?
options: Rows are stored in insertion order, so row 42 is at a known position
The database caches the result of every query
Comparing integers is so fast that scanning 10 million rows is instant
The database keeps an index on the primary key automatically
why: To enforce uniqueness quickly, databases back a primary key (and a UNIQUE constraint) with an index, and that same index serves lookups by id. Foreign key columns, by contrast, are often not indexed automatically.
wrong: Ids are not file offsets: rows get deleted, ids can have gaps, and storage order is not guaranteed.
A cache cannot explain a fast first lookup. The speed comes from the index behind the key.
A scan still reads every row. A fast comparison does not turn O(n) into a few steps.

q: A transfer runs in one transaction: subtract 100 from account A, then add 100 to B. The server crashes between the two updates. After restart, what is stored?
options: A is 100 lower and B is unchanged, so someone must fix it by hand
Neither change: the subtraction from A is undone
Both changes: the database finishes the transfer on restart
A is 100 lower, and B gets the 100 the next time someone reads it
why: Atomicity means a transaction happens completely or not at all. This one never committed, so during recovery the database rolls its changes back, and both accounts look as they did before the transfer.
wrong: That is what happens without a transaction. Inside one, an unfinished change is rolled back.
The database cannot know how to finish your work. It undoes changes that were never committed.
Nothing is deferred to later reads. The uncommitted subtraction simply does not survive.

q: COMMIT returns success, and a second later the server loses power. After restart the change is still there. Which ACID property promises this?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
why: Durability means a committed transaction stays committed, even after a crash or power loss. Databases usually achieve it by writing the change to a log on disk before they report success.
wrong: Atomicity is about all or nothing inside a transaction, not about surviving a crash after the commit.
Consistency is about the data obeying its rules and constraints before and after a transaction.
Isolation is about concurrent transactions not seeing each other's unfinished work.

q: balance has CHECK (balance >= 0). A transfer would leave one account at -20, so the whole transaction fails. Which idea does this show?
options: Consistency: data only moves from one valid state to another
Consistency: every replica returns the same value at the same moment
Isolation: other transactions must not see the -20
Durability: the database refused to store a value it could not keep
why: Consistency in ACID means each committed transaction leaves the data valid under the rules the database knows: keys, constraints, checks. A rule that lives only in app code is not enforced by the database.
wrong: That is the C in CAP, about copies on several servers. The C in ACID is about rules on the data.
Isolation is about concurrent transactions. Here a rule would break even with a single user.
Durability is about committed data surviving crashes, not about which values are allowed.

q: Two requests run at once, with no explicit transaction. Each reads stock = 10, subtracts 1 in app code, then runs UPDATE items SET stock = 9 WHERE id = 1. What is the final stock?
options: 8, because the database applies both updates in turn
It depends on which request writes first: 9 or 8
9, because one of the two sales is lost
An error, because the database sees the row changed after it was read
why: This is a lost update. Both requests read 10 before either wrote, so both compute 9, and the second write overwrites the first. Nothing tells the database the two decrements were meant to stack.
wrong: It does apply both, but each writes the fixed value 9, computed from the same old read.
Either order gives 9, since both requests write a value computed from the same read of 10.
The database cannot know the app read the row earlier. It just runs two valid UPDATE statements.

q: Many requests sell the same item by reading stock, subtracting 1 in app code, and writing it back. Some sales get lost. What is the simplest reliable fix?
options: Read the stock twice and write only if both reads agree
UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 1
Add an index on the stock column
Have each request wait a short random delay before writing
why: With stock = stock - 1, the database reads the current value and writes the new one in a single step that no other write can slip into. Concurrent decrements take turns, so none is lost. Locking the row when reading, or a version check, also work.
wrong: Another request can still write between the second read and your write. The gap only gets smaller.
An index speeds up finding rows. It does nothing about two requests racing on the same row.
Random delays make the race rarer and harder to reproduce, not impossible.

q: Placing an order inserts a row into orders, inserts its lines into order_items, and lowers stock. Why run the three statements in one transaction?
options: So a failure halfway cannot leave an order without its items
Because INSERT only works inside an explicit transaction
So other users see each step as soon as it runs
To lock the whole database so nobody can read during the order
why: The three changes only make sense together. Inside a transaction, if any statement fails, a ROLLBACK (or crash recovery) undoes the others, so the database never holds an order with no items or sold stock that was never subtracted.
wrong: Each statement runs fine on its own in autocommit mode. The problem is the half-done state between them.
It is the opposite: other sessions see the changes only at commit, all together.
A transaction does not normally block all readers. Its job is to make the group of changes all or nothing.

q: The session starts in autocommit mode with no transaction open. Account 1 has 100 and account 2 has 50. What does the final SELECT show?
why: Before BEGIN, each statement is its own transaction and commits at once, so the -30 is permanent. BEGIN opens a transaction holding the +30, and ROLLBACK discards it. The 30 vanished: the transfer had to start with BEGIN to be atomic.
wrong: ROLLBACK only undoes work since BEGIN. The first UPDATE ran in autocommit mode and was committed on its own.
ROLLBACK does undo the second UPDATE. Only committed work survives it.
ROLLBACK does not reach back to the last committed statement. It discards the open transaction, which holds only the +30.

q: A users table needs a primary key column. What must be true of the values in that column?
options: They are auto-incrementing integers
They are unique, though one row may hold NULL
They may repeat, as long as the other columns differ
Each is unique in the table, and none is NULL
why: A primary key is how each row is identified, so two rows cannot share a key value and no row may lack one. A table has one primary key, which may span several columns, and the database indexes it.
wrong: Auto-increment is a common way to fill a key, but a product code or an email can be a key too.
A primary key identifies every row, so NULL is not allowed. Accepting NULLs is a trait of UNIQUE.
A key that spans several columns is a composite key, and then that whole combination must be unique.

q: orders.customer_id is a foreign key referencing customers.id. What does this constraint guarantee?
options: Each customer_id appears at most once in orders
Queries on orders automatically include the customer's columns
Each non-NULL customer_id matches an existing customer
A customer row can never be deleted
why: A foreign key enforces referential integrity: you cannot insert an order for a customer that does not exist, or delete a customer that orders still point to (unless the key says to cascade). It does not limit how many orders refer to one customer.
wrong: That is a UNIQUE constraint. A foreign key allows many orders per customer.
A foreign key does not join anything. You still write the JOIN.
Deleting is blocked only while orders still point to it, and the key can be set to cascade or set NULL instead.

q: A student takes many courses, and a course has many students. How should the tables model this?
options: A course_id column in students, pointing at the course they take
A junction table, enrollments(student_id, course_id)
A courses column in students holding a list like '3,7,12'
A student_id column in courses, pointing at the enrolled student
why: A foreign key column holds one value, so it models one-to-many. Many-to-many needs a junction table: each row links one student to one course, with a foreign key to each and the pair as its key.
wrong: One column holds one value, so each student could take only one course.
A list in one cell breaks first normal form: you cannot join, index or constrain the individual ids.
One column holds one value, so each course could have only one student.

q: orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_city, total) repeats the city on every order. A customer moves and only some rows get updated. What is the design fix?
options: Move the city to customers; it depends on the customer, not the order
Keep it: repeated data always makes reads faster, so it is the better design
Add an index on customer_city
Add customer_city to the primary key of orders
why: customer_city is a fact about the customer, reached through customer_id, not about the order. Storing it per order invites update anomalies like this one. Third normal form, in plain terms: every non-key column describes the key and nothing else.
wrong: Copies can speed up some reads, but they must be kept in sync, and that is exactly the bug here.
An index speeds up searches. It does nothing to keep the copies in agreement.
A bigger key does not make the copies agree. The city simply does not belong to the order.

q: Each order belongs to one customer, and a customer can have many orders. Where does the foreign key go?
options: customers.order_id, referencing orders
In both tables, each pointing at the other
In a separate customer_orders link table
orders.customer_id, referencing customers
why: In one-to-many, the key goes on the many side. Each order row stores the one customer it belongs to, and a customer's orders are simply the rows that hold its id.
wrong: One column in customers holds one order id, so each customer could have only one order.
Two links store the same fact twice, and the copies can disagree. One side is enough.
A link table is for many-to-many. Here it adds a join and would even let one order belong to several customers.

q: A payments service records money moving between accounts and must never lose or double-count a transfer. Which store fits best?
options: An in-memory key-value cache, for its speed
A document store, since it needs no fixed schema
A relational database, with transactions and constraints
A graph database, since transfers link accounts together
why: A transfer touches several rows that must change together and obey rules (no negative balance, valid accounts). Relational databases offer multi-row transactions, foreign keys and checks, which is what a ledger needs.
wrong: A cache may drop data on restart or eviction. It is not a system of record for money.
Schema flexibility is not the need here. Atomic changes to several rows, with rules enforced, are.
Transfers do form a graph, but the critical need is atomic, constrained updates, a core strength of relational databases.

q: A store sells shoes, laptops and books, each with its own set of attributes, and a page usually loads one whole product. What fits naturally?
options: A pure key-value store, because each product has an id
A document store, one document per product with its own fields
One relational table with a column for every attribute of every category
A graph database, because products relate to categories
why: Each product is read as one unit and the fields vary by category, which suits documents. A relational design is still possible (an attribute table or a JSON column); the question is fit, not that SQL cannot do it.
wrong: A key-value store fetches by key only. A catalog also needs to filter and search by product fields.
It works, but most columns are NULL in most rows, and each new attribute needs a schema change.
Almost every model has relations. Graph stores pay off when queries walk links, like friends of friends.

q: A team picks a document database so they never have to think about schema. A year later, what are they most likely dealing with?
options: Nothing, since the database tracks each shape and migrates old documents itself
Slow lookups on every field, since a schemaless store cannot have indexes
Nothing, since NoSQL databases stay fast for any query by design
Code that must cope with old documents whose fields are missing or renamed
why: Dropping the schema from the database moves it into the code. Every reader still expects certain fields and types, so changing a shape means handling old documents or migrating them by hand. Many teams add schema validation back for this reason.
wrong: The database stores what it is given. Reshaping old documents is the team's job.
Document stores do support indexes on fields.
Speed depends on fitting the data model and indexes to the queries. A query the model was not built for can still be slow.
